problem: Existing embodied navigation methods are built for one task (VLN, ObjectNav, EQA or following) with task-specific modules and data, so they cannot share skills across tasks. LLM-based generalists fall short in two ways. Prompting approaches work on discretized landmark graphs and text scene descriptions at low inference frequency. Video-based VLAs such as NaVid slow down to 1–2 s per step as the number of history-frame tokens grows, which makes continuous real-world deployment impractical.
motivation: A practical robot must handle many kinds of navigation instructions in continuous, dynamic real environments, using only cheap sensors and running fast enough to act without stopping. The paper's premise has three parts: recent frames matter most for navigation, consecutive frames are highly redundant, and pooling heterogeneous navigation data plus internet video QA into one end-to-end VLA should give cross-task synergy and better sim-to-real generalization.
key_idea: Train one video-based VLA (EVA-CLIP + Vicuna-7B) on 3.6M multi-task navigation samples plus 2.3M video-QA samples. An online current/short-term/long-term token-merging memory keeps the token count small enough to predict 4 low-level actions per call at about 5 Hz from monocular RGB video alone.
insight: Memory structure is what makes history-dependent tasks work. With only current-frame tokens, VLN SR falls from 48.7 to 9.61 (−80.3%); adding short-term memory recovers it to 39.7 and adding long-term memory to 48.7. Human following barely changes (56.3 vs 61.2) because it relies on recent frames. Co-training with VQA data is essential: without it, EQA accuracy collapses to 1.19 and ObjectNav SR drops from 73.7 to 50.6, which the authors attribute to catastrophic forgetting. Without the <NAV> task token, EQA falls to 20.4 because the model confuses answering with acting. Data quality also matters. ObjectNav trained on shortest-path demos reaches only 30.1% SR, versus 73.7 with exploratory L3MVN trajectories. A multi-task vs single-task comparison (shown only in a figure) indicates gains on all tasks, largest on VLN, ObjectNav and EQA. Scaling from 3M to 6M samples gives diminishing returns.
method: Observation encoding: each egocentric RGB frame is encoded by EVA-CLIP into 256 patch tokens; training videos are sampled at 1 FPS.

Online visual token merging (Atkinson-Shiffrin-style memory): the current frame is grid-pooled to 64 tokens (α=2). The last B=64 frames form short-term memory at 4 tokens each (α=8); older frames become 1 long-term token each (α=16). A new long-term token is averaged into the previous one (weighted by its merge count K) when cosine similarity > τ=0.95, otherwise appended. Updates are incremental, so only tokens at group boundaries are re-pooled at each step.

Action planning with LLM: a 2-layer MLP projector maps the merged tokens into Vicuna-7B. The input is [long][short][current] + <NAV> + instruction, with frame-separator tokens between frames. The LLM outputs 4 action tokens from {FORWARD 25 cm, TURN-LEFT/RIGHT 30°, STOP}; the episode stops if the first predicted action is STOP. Inference takes about 0.2 s per call.

Multi-task navigation data (3.6M samples, Habitat, HM3D+MP3D, 861 scenes): VLN-CE R2R+RxR 2.4M (0.64M GT trajectories, 1.69M DAgger with a fast-marching expert, 70k low-level-action instructions); HM3D ObjectNav 483k from successful L3MVN rollouts; MP3D-EQA 240k action samples + 10k answer samples; 544k samples from a new language-described human-following benchmark on Habitat 3.0/HM3D with 2–6 distractor humans. ChatGPT rephrases instructions for diversity.

Training: stage 1 aligns the projector on LLaMA-VID data. Stage 2 fine-tunes projector + LLM for 1 epoch on the 3.6M navigation samples plus 2.3M video QA/captioning samples (ScanQA, Panda-70M, LLaMA-VID), with token merging also applied to VQA samples. Compute is 40 H800 GPUs × ~35 h.
Task switching for EQA: the agent navigates with <NAV> until STOP, then <NAV> is removed and the question is asked over the navigation history.

Non-blocking real-world deployment: the model runs on a remote A100 while the Unitree Go2 uploads compressed frames asynchronously. The robot always executes the latest 4-action chunk through Unitree's local motion controller.

numbers_note: Several results appear only in figures, with no numbers: multi-task vs single-task synergy, data-scale curves, inference-time comparison, and real-world statistics for tasks other than VLN. The ablation table (Curr./Short/Long memory, no <NAV>, no VQA; τ and token-count ablations) reports VLN SR 48.7 for the full model, which matches the RxR-CE number, so the ablation VLN column is apparently RxR-CE; these ablation variants are not listed as separate entries. The text contains inconsistent claims. It says RxR is '+3.6 SR' over R2R, but the tables give 48.7 vs 47.0. The '+25.7%' SR over NaVid on R2R and '+4.7% SR / +8.8% SPL' on ObjectNav are relative gains, not absolute. An intro placeholder claims RxR 36%→52%. The LaTeX contains duplicated draft sections and duplicated tables, and the data-collection text says R2R/RxR are 'within the HM3D datasets', although VLN-CE uses MP3D scenes. Split names for the human-following, ScanQA and video-QA benchmarks are not stated in the paper and were assigned here.
results: With monocular RGB only, Uni-NaVid reaches R2R-CE val-unseen SR 47.0 / SPL 42.7, beating NaVid (37.4/35.9) and other low-level-action methods, though it stays below panoramic waypoint methods such as ETPNav (57.0/49.0). It reaches RxR-CE SR 48.7 / SPL 40.9, versus ETPNav.FF 25.5 SR and NaVid 23.8; without RxR training data it still gets 29.5. On HM3D ObjectNav it reports SR 73.7 / SPL 37.1 versus PIRLNav-IL-RL 70.4/34.1. Zero-shot on HM3D-OVON val-unseen it gets 39.5/19.8, versus fine-tuned DAgRL+OD 37.1/19.8 and VLFM 35.2/19.6. On MP3D-EQA it scores 47.3 ACC vs NaviLLM 44.5, and on its new language-described human-following benchmark 61.21 SR vs IBVS with GT boxes at 50.58. It also stays competitive on video QA (ActivityNet-QA 51.4) and runs at about 0.2 s per 4-action inference.
limitations: Covers only four well-defined navigation tasks trained purely on simulated Habitat data; gains saturate from 3M to 6M samples, which the authors attribute to limited simulator diversity. No RL fine-tuning is used.

Assumes a standard-size robot embodiment and outputs only short horizons of coarse discrete actions (25 cm / 30°), not smooth continuous trajectories. Real-world use needs a remote A100 server plus about 0.3 s of network latency.

Several comparisons are not like-for-like: RxR baselines were trained only on R2R, the human-following benchmark is self-built and trained on the same HM3D source, and the paper states a 30° turn for all tasks, versus the standard 15° turn in R2R-CE.
